source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert study of research ideas: LLM ideas were rated more novel than human-expert ideas. Design: 49 human ideas, 49 AI ideas, 49 AI ideas hand-reranked by a human; 79 expert reviewers wrote 298 unique reviews.
numbers: Idea-level novelty (1-10): human 4.86, AI 5.62 (p=0.03), AI+human rerank 5.78 (p<0.01). Review-level overall score: human 4.68, AI 4.85 (n.s.), rerank 5.34 (p=0.04). 72 of 79 reviewers had reviewed for major venues.
quote: AI ideas are judged as significantly better than human ideas in terms of novelty and excitement while being comparable on all other metrics.
limits: Judged before any execution. Only NLP prompting topics. Human ideas were written by experts in a short time, not their best ideas. Novelty is rated, not measured.
agent_relevance: A novelty score from raters is a weak signal: it later flipped under execution (see the Ideation-Execution Gap lines). Do not treat a high novelty rating as success.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Reviewers' overall score tracks novelty and excitement, not feasibility.
numbers: Correlation of overall score with novelty r=0.725, with excitement r=0.854, with feasibility r<0.1.
limits: Correlations among ratings by the same reviewers, so partly one halo of taste.
agent_relevance: Judged quality of ideas is mostly a novelty-and-excitement halo. A selector built on such scores will reward showy ideas and ignore whether they work (supports G8).

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Human reviewers agree only a little on idea quality. LLM judges agree with the human consensus even less, at or below chance.
numbers: Split-half agreement of reviewers on top/bottom 25% of ideas: 56.1%. Benchmarks: NeurIPS 2021 66.0%, ICLR 2024 71.9%. LLM judges on the same task: GPT-4o direct 50.0%, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7%, Claude-3.5 pairwise 53.3%, AI Scientist reviewer 43.3%.
limits: Balanced top/bottom 25% task, small sample (49 ideas per condition). Authors note drops versus earlier published LLM-reviewer agreement figures.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G8: a model that grades ideas cannot be the selector. Even the human ceiling is low (56%), so any rater score needs many raters or an execution check.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Generating more LLM ideas does not give more distinct ideas. The pool collapses to near-duplicates.
numbers: Of 4000 generated seed ideas per topic, only about 5% (about 200) remained after removing ideas with embedding similarity above 0.8 to an earlier idea; the count of new unique ideas plateaued as generation continued.
limits: Dedup threshold 0.8 chosen by manual inspection; embedding similarity is itself a crude novelty measure.
agent_relevance: An automatic novelty filter (embedding distance to earlier ideas and to prior art) is cheap, runnable, and finds real duplication. Use it to measure coverage before spending tokens on judging. Links to the quality-diversity subfield.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Follow-up randomized trial: the same ideas were executed by experts into full projects and re-reviewed blind. AI ideas lost their lead on every metric. Rankings flipped (not significant at idea level).
numbers: 43 execution participants (66 onboarded, 3 months, 20 USD/h plus 600 USD bonus); 58 reviewers; 181 execution reviews. Novelty ideation vs execution: human 4.912 -> 4.903, AI 5.778 -> 4.729. Excitement: human 4.404 -> 4.482, AI 5.653 -> 3.896. Effectiveness: human 4.833 -> 4.782, AI 6.003 -> 4.125. Overall: human 4.596 -> 3.968, AI 5.382 -> 3.406.
quote: AI ideas' scores drop significantly more than human ideas in the execution evaluation across all four metrics
limits: Review-level one-sided tests were significant for excitement, effectiveness, soundness and overall, not novelty; idea-level (N=43) differences between conditions were not significant, so the pre-registered hypothesis was not confirmed. The gap itself (pre vs post) was significant (p<0.05).
agent_relevance: The strongest evidence that execution beats opinion as a validator of ideas. A scaffold should prefer runnable tests of an idea over any judged score (G8, G3).

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Score changes after execution: human ideas keep their scores, AI ideas lose a lot.
numbers: Mean change on 1-10 scale: human novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052; AI novelty -1.049, excitement -1.760, effectiveness -1.879.
limits: Reviewers see more evidence in executed work, and AI ideas may rely on vague claims that fail when made concrete. 6 of 43 ideas swapped a planned human evaluation for LLM judging; removing them did not change the result.
agent_relevance: Judged novelty at proposal time overstates real value for model-written ideas. Re-score after a cheap prototype, not before.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Pre-execution and post-execution scores barely correlate. For AI ideas, the correlation for excitement is moderately negative.
numbers: Appendix D reports weak correlations between ideation and execution scores in most cases; AI excitement correlation is moderately negative (exact value not extracted).
limits: Small N (43 projects). Exact coefficients in appendix tables were not read.
agent_relevance: Proposal-stage judged scores have little predictive validity for outcomes. Do not rank ideas by them without a run.

source: Falk, Chen, Rafner, Zhang, Bjerva, Nolte (2025) How Do Hackathons Foster Creativity? Towards AI Collaborative Evaluation of Creativity at Scale
finding: Small open LLMs used as novelty and usefulness judges on hackathon projects show strong central-tendency and level biases that differ by model.
numbers: On 21,318 project descriptions sampled from 193,353: Gemma-2-9b-it gave score 3 for about 80% of novelty and about 75% of usefulness; Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B peaked at 4 (about 65%); Prometheus-7B spread over 2-5. Usefulness scores exceeded novelty scores for all models.
limits: Small judge models, no ground truth for this part. Descriptions are text of varying length.
agent_relevance: Judge calibration differs by model, so raw scores are not comparable across judges. Use ranks or pairwise comparison inside one judge, never absolute scores.

source: Falk, Chen, Rafner, Zhang, Bjerva, Nolte (2025) How Do Hackathons Foster Creativity? Towards AI Collaborative Evaluation of Creativity at Scale
finding: Two experienced human raters disagreed on novelty almost completely, and agreed more on usefulness. LLM-human agreement was higher for usefulness than novelty.
numbers: 30 projects, 2 human raters, Cohen's kappa. Human-human novelty: 0.18 (scores bucketed 1-3 vs 4-5) falling to 0.04 on the full scale. Human-human usefulness 0.53 (2 buckets), 0.12 (full scale). Best kappas: Prometheus and Llama 0.59 for novelty (between LLMs), Mistral and Llama 0.46 for usefulness, Human 1 with Llama 0.42 (2 buckets).
limits: n=30, two raters, tiny kappas with wide intervals. LLM-LLM agreement can be high through shared biases, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Novelty is the least reliable axis even among humans. Treat any single novelty score as noisy and require repeated or multi-rater scoring.

source: Ritchie (2007) Some Empirical Criteria for Attributing Creativity to a Computer Program
finding: Formal framework with observable properties of an output set R: typicality (how much an item belongs to the genre), quality (value), and the inspiring set I the program drew on. Creativity is judged from ratings plus set overlap, with no claims about inner process.
numbers: 14 original criteria (from Ritchie 2001): e.g. C1-2 average and share of typical items, C3-4 average and share of high-quality items, C5-8 quality among typical and untypical items, C9-10 overlap of R with I, C11-14 typicality and quality of the novel items (R minus I). Revised versions 8a and 10a, plus new 15-18. Parameters alpha, beta (typicality bounds), gamma (quality threshold), theta (comparison level).
quote: Quality: To what extent is the produced item a high quality example of its genre?
limits: Thresholds are unprincipled (applications set them to 0.5 with no reason). Needs human typicality and value ratings. Overlap with I is set membership only, not graded similarity; the author names this the main weakness.
agent_relevance: Gives a runnable shape for an idea-pool audit: separate novel items (not in prior art) from copies, then ask what share of the novel ones are valuable. Needs only counts once typicality and value are scored.

source: Ritchie (2007) Some Empirical Criteria for Attributing Creativity to a Computer Program
finding: Applications of Ritchie's criteria reinterpreted the key terms. Typicality was taken as the opposite of originality, and value as fit to the program's own goal, making some tests fully algorithmic.
numbers: Dupond paraphrase study: 192 items, humans rated generated sentences on 3-point scales for originality, same meaning, comprehensibility; alpha, beta, gamma all set to 0.5. Haenen and Rauchas: 21 melodies. In the WASP study no item from the inspiring set appeared in the results, so criteria 9-14 were not informative.
limits: Ritchie warns users treated the 14 criteria as an equal-weight checklist, which was not intended. Empty overlap with the inspiring set makes several criteria vacuous.
agent_relevance: When a task has a computable value (a test passes), the framework collapses to a search with a clear score. Creative scoring is needed only where value has no check.

source: Jordanous (2013) Evaluating Computational Creativity: A Standardised Procedure for Evaluating Creative Systems and its Application (PhD thesis, University of Sussex; SPECS)
finding: SPECS is a three-step procedure: (1) define creativity for the domain, (2) state the standards you will test against, (3) run tests and report. Step 1 is filled by 14 empirically derived components of creativity.
numbers: 14 components, e.g. Active Involvement and Persistence; Generation of Results; Dealing with Uncertainty; Domain Competence; General Intellect; Independence and Freedom; Originality; Social Interaction and Communication; Spontaneity and Subconscious Processing; Variety, Divergence and Experimentation; Intention and Emotional Involvement. Derived from corpus analysis of creativity discourse plus a survey of people.
limits: Weights per component are chosen by the evaluator, so results are not comparable across projects. The domain-specific step needs expert input.
agent_relevance: Useful as a checklist for what an open-mode output must show, but it is a procedure for people, not a scorer. The components testable by code are Variety, Divergence and Generation of Results.

source: Jordanous (2013) Evaluating Computational Creativity: A Standardised Procedure for Evaluating Creative Systems and its Application (PhD thesis, University of Sussex; SPECS)
finding: Meta-evaluation of SPECS against Ritchie's criteria, Colton's creative tripod, FACE and a plain opinion survey, using system builders as evaluators. The survey of human opinion was rated least correct.
numbers: Case Study 1: musical improvisation systems; evaluators Al Biles (all methods), George Lewis (SPECS and tripod), Bob Keller (comments). SPECS and tripod rated extremely useful by both Biles and Lewis; SPECS and Ritchie 'quite correct'; opinion survey numbers 'a bit mushy' and lowest correctness.
quote: the numeric results `were a bit mushy'
limits: Three evaluators, 5-point scales, evaluators knew their own systems. Biles called SPECS 'not very user-friendly'.
agent_relevance: Asking people 'is it creative?' without a definition gave the least trusted numbers. A stated rubric, even coarse, beats an unguided score.

source: Jordanous (2013) Evaluating Computational Creativity: A Standardised Procedure for Evaluating Creative Systems and its Application (PhD thesis, University of Sussex; SPECS)
finding: The thesis surveys the other founding definitions: creativity as novelty plus value, Boden's three types, Colton's creative tripod (skill, imagination, appreciation, as perceived by an audience), and process-aware evaluation.
numbers: Most cited definitions pair novelty with usefulness (Mayer 1999 table of seven authors incl. Boden: novel and valuable). Plucker et al. 2004: 34 of 90 surveyed articles gave a definition; uniqueness appeared in 24, usefulness in 17, and all 17 that named usefulness also named novelty.
limits: Secondary reading of Boden, Colton and Plucker through the thesis, not their original papers. Boden's surprise criterion is only touched on here.
agent_relevance: Definitions all need a reference class for novelty. In our agent that class is the model's own earlier ideas and retrieved prior art, which we can compute.

source: Beaty and Johnson (2021) Automating creativity assessment with SemDis: An open platform for computing semantic distance
finding: Semantic distance (distance between prompt and response word vectors) predicts human creativity ratings of Alternate Uses Task answers at the latent-variable level.
numbers: Five studies. Study 1 (N=171, AUT): latent semantic-distance factor vs latent human creativity r=.91. Study 2: r=.75 latent. Study 4 (word association): latent semantic distance vs novelty ratings r=.95, single models GloVe .97, cbowukwac .96, TASA .92. Study 5: latent vs originality about r=.85.
limits: Latent correlations remove measurement error and are higher than response-level correlations. Elaboration bias: longer responses got lower distance, but humans rated longer responses as more creative (r=.41 word count vs rating). A multiplicative composition reduced the bias but did not remove it.
agent_relevance: A cheap, runnable novelty-by-distance measure exists and tracks human originality for short answers. Pair it with a length control and a relevance check, since distance also rewards nonsense.

source: Buczak, Huang, Forthmann, Doebler (2022) The Machines Take Over: A Comparison of Various Supervised Learning Approaches for Automated Scoring of Divergent Thinking Tasks
finding: Supervised models (random forest, XGBoost, SVR) on word-embedding features predict human originality ratings. Longer answers and answers semantically distant from the object get higher ratings.
numbers: Two lab data sets (Hofelich-Mohr 2016, Silvia 2008). Cross-sample correlations: RF .57 to .58 and XGBoost .59 to .64 on Silvia data; RF .76 to .78 on a further validation and .59 to .60 on Hofelich-Mohr data. Models beat the mean-rating RMSE baseline in nested resampling.
limits: Cross-sample RMSE hard to improve because of rater mean differences; scoring tied to item type.
agent_relevance: Word count alone is a strong predictor of rated originality. Any automated or judged novelty score in our agent must be length-controlled (G5).

source: Organisciak, Acar, Dumas, Berthiaume (2023) Beyond semantic distance: Automated scoring of divergent thinking greatly improves with large language models
finding: Fine-tuned language models score Alternate Uses answers much better than semantic distance, and transfer to new items. Known only from search snippets and a project page, not the paper.
numbers: Up to r=.81 with human raters versus r=.12 to .26 for earlier systems; 27 thousand responses from nine past studies (as relayed by search, not checked).
limits: Numbers not verified in the paper text this session. Trained on human labels for short answers.
agent_relevance: Supervised scorers trained on human labels beat distance measures for short ideas, but need labelled data; this does not show that an untrained judge model works.

source: Kaufman, Baer, Cole, Sexton (2008) A Comparison of Expert and Nonexpert Raters Using the Consensual Assessment Technique
finding: Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT) with 10 expert poets versus 106 nonexperts rating 205 college-student poems. Experts agreed; nonexperts did not once rater count was equalised, and the two groups' mean ratings barely matched.
numbers: Raw coefficient alpha: experts .832 (10 raters), nonexperts .935 (106 raters). Standardised to 10 raters with Spearman-Brown: experts .804, nonexperts .575. Correlation of group mean ratings .21 (4.41% shared variance). Group means: novices 4.47 (SD .87), experts 3.09 (SD .90).
quote: Nonexpert raters' judgments of creativity were inconsistent (showing low interrater reliability) and did not match those of the expert raters.
limits: One domain (poetry), student poems, no rubric. Raw alpha rises with rater count, so equal-size comparison is the fair one.
agent_relevance: Competence matters more than rater count. A weak judge model is the nonexpert case: its many votes can look consistent while missing expert opinion.

source: Baer, Kaufman, Gentile (2004) Extension of the Consensual Assessment Technique to Nonparallel Creative Products
finding: CAT reliability holds even when the products were written to different prompts, so ratings can compare across tasks. Expert ratings are made independently with no rubric.
numbers: 13 expert judges; coefficient alpha .940 for stories, .957 for personal narratives, .868 for poems. Pairwise inter-rater correlations: poems .61 to .72 (mean .66), stories .73 to .81 (mean .76), personal narratives .78 to .80 (mean .79). Prior CAT work: alphas usually above .70, often up to .90s.
limits: Alpha is inflated by using 13 raters; the pairwise correlations are the conservative figures. Writing by 8th graders; raters read by mail.
agent_relevance: With enough competent raters, creativity ratings are reliable (alpha .87 to .96) even though single pairs agree only at r .66 to .79. This is the human ground truth LLM judges are compared with.

source: Kaufman, Christopher, Kaufman (2008) The Genius Portfolio: How Do Poets Earn Their Creative Reputations From Multiple Products?
finding: Experts rating a set of five poems by one poet: the set's overall rating followed the average, best, worst and last poem, but not the variability.
numbers: 10 expert raters in 2 independent groups, 4 sets each (N=40 sets per group); the mean of the five poems explained 74% of overall-rating variance in rater group 1 and 92% in group 2; correlation among rating dimensions at least .77 (group 1) and .89 (group 2). Pulitzer-winning poet sets rated higher (3.67 and 3.78 vs 3.05 and 2.82).
limits: Poetry only. Gender effects on ratings were unstable between the two rater groups.
agent_relevance: How a set of ideas is aggregated into one judgment matters. Mean quality was the main driver; consistency did not matter. For an idea pool, report the average and the best, not the variance.

source: Clements, Redding, Lefebvre Sell, May (2018) Expertise in Evaluating Choreographic Creativity: An Online Variation of the Consensual Assessment Technique
finding: A large online CAT variant: raters' own creative or choreographic experience shifted their creativity ratings, so rater background is a bias source.
numbers: 23 dance videos, 850 online evaluators (from 1084 recruited), 7-point scales; one-way ANOVA showed creativity differs across videos; contemporary choreography experience and self-reported creative expertise predicted ratings; inter-rater reliability correlation 0.83 reported for one subgroup.
limits: Videos were rated by random subsets, so classic alpha could not be used. Self-reported expertise. Domain far from text.
agent_relevance: Judge identity shapes the score. For model judges the model, persona and prompt are part of the instrument and must be fixed and logged.

source: Chakrabarty, Laban, Agarwal, Muresan, Wu (2024) Art or Artifice? Large Language Models and the False Promise of Creativity
finding: 14 binary Torrance-style tests for stories (TTCW) over fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration. Experts agree moderately on single tests and well on the total. LLMs fail to reproduce expert answers.
numbers: 48 stories (12 human New Yorker stories, 36 LLM stories), 10 experts, 2000+ tests. Fleiss kappa 0.41 across tests; Pearson 0.69 on aggregated test counts. Human stories passed 84.7% of tests; GPT-3.5 stories under 10%, GPT-4 and Claude v1.3 about 30% (3 to 10 times fewer). LLM-as-judge correlation with experts close to zero; GPT-4 above 0.2 on only 2 of 14 tests.
limits: Zero-shot judge prompts; few-shot attempts on a couple of tests gave no significant gain. Long stories, 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Binary expert-style tests aggregate to a reliable score, but the model judge does not reproduce them on long outputs. Use code-checkable tests, not model-administered ones (G8).

source: Sawicki, Grzes, Brown, Goes (2025) Can Large Language Models Outperform Non-Experts in Poetry Evaluation? A Comparative Study Using the Consensual Assessment Technique
finding: Re-evaluated the Lamb et al. (2015) 90-poem set where crowd raters inverted the ground truth. Forced-choice ranking in small batches makes LLMs far better than non-experts and very consistent.
numbers: Ground truth: publication venue (Good/Medium/Bad). Non-expert humans: Quality SRC -0.33, Skill -0.35, Wellbeing and Effort -0.45; only Novelty positive, SRC 0.38 (best human result). LLMs: best Quality SRC 0.87 (Claude-3-Opus, batches of 15 poems, rank-derived scores); GPT-4o 0.62 in the first experiment; ranking all 90 poems at once was worse (best about 0.68); ICCk reliabilities high.
limits: Ground truth is venue prestige, not creativity ratings. Only poetry. Batch size and scoring method were tuned on the same 90 poems, so some overfit is possible.
agent_relevance: A model judge works when it ranks a few items against each other, with randomized order and batches, and the ground truth is external. Fits G5: compare items, do not score one item alone.

source: LitBench authors (2025) LitBench: A Benchmark and Dataset for Reliable Evaluation of Creative Writing
finding: Human-preference benchmark from Reddit story pairs. Zero-shot LLM judges reach about 73%; reward models trained on the pairs reach 78%. Chain of thought lowers accuracy.
numbers: Test set 2,480 debiased human-labelled story comparisons; train 43,827 pairs. Claude-3.7-Sonnet 73% (best zero-shot); Bradley-Terry Llama-8B 78%; generative reward model with CoT 72%; small open models 56-60%. Raw data had 65.25% of chosen stories longer, so pairs were pruned to balance length. Online check: 46 crowd workers preferred the reward model's pick 57% vs 41%; the best LLM judge performed at chance there.
limits: Ground truth is Reddit upvotes (with a 25% vote-gap filter and timing control), i.e. popularity, not expert creativity.
agent_relevance: Length bias is large and must be removed from judging data (G5). Reasoning made judges worse, which supports short direct comparisons.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Humanlike Diversity
finding: Novelty measured as the count of functionally distinct answers over k samples, not by a judge's opinion. A trained pairwise equivalence classifier groups outputs; utility combines novelty and quality with a patience weight.
numbers: Equivalence classifier (deberta-v3-large, 1,000 training pairs) reached 79% accuracy, F1 0.811 on 100 held-out human-labelled pairs; BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore diverged from human judgment. Patience p=0.8. With in-context regeneration, Claude 3 Opus, GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro roughly matched human-writer diversity (8 authors as baseline, 100 curated prompts, 8 generations); GPT-4o and Gemini exceeded human utility. Paraphrase and system-prompt tricks helped only a little. Larger models in a family often less diverse.
limits: Human baseline is the 8 paper authors (homogeneous). Quality uses a reward model. Functional equivalence is defined by user value, a judgment call.
agent_relevance: A measured, repeatable diversity metric that avoids rating novelty on a scale. Showing the model its own earlier answers is the lever. Links to the quality-diversity subfield.

source: Wu et al. (2026) NovBench: Evaluating Large Language Models on Academic Paper Novelty Assessment
finding: Benchmark of 1,684 paper-review pairs from an NLP venue to test whether LLMs, including review-tuned ones, can write novelty evaluations like expert reviewers, with four dimensions (relevance, correctness, coverage, clarity).
numbers: 1,684 paper-review pairs; compared CycleReviewer-70B/8B, DeepReviewer-14B/7B, Llama-OpenReviewer-8B, Reviewer2, with human reviewer rows. Review-tuned models differ widely on the metrics; humans score lower on relevance because reviews also cover other topics.
limits: Only the abstract, set-up and one results table were read; no single headline number was extracted. Metrics compare to reviewer text, which is not ground truth for real novelty.
agent_relevance: Judging novelty from text rewards imitating reviewer prose. Prefer retrieval of prior art (does a close work exist) over generated opinions.

source: Lamb, Brown, Clarke (2015) Can human assessment of machine-generated poetry be trusted? (as reported in Sawicki et al. 2025)
finding: Crowd raters ranked a 90-poem set backwards: professionally published poems lowest, amateur poems highest. Known only through Sawicki et al.
numbers: Non-expert Quality SRC -0.33 with the venue ground truth; Novelty SRC 0.38 (from Sawicki's Table 1).
limits: Second-hand. Original paper not opened.
agent_relevance: A human crowd can be systematically wrong, so human-rated alone is not validity. Judge validity needs an external criterion.

source: Kaufman, Baer, Cole (2009) Expertise, domains, and the consensual assessment technique (as reported by search summaries)
finding: Expert-novice comparison on short fiction: novices and experts correlated .71 but experts were far more consistent. Only seen in a search summary.
numbers: Correlation .71 between novice and expert mean ratings (search summary).
limits: Not opened. Contrasts with the poetry result of .21 (Kaufman et al. 2008), so agreement depends on domain.
agent_relevance: Judge competence depends on task type. Check agreement with an expert reference per task class before trusting a cheap judge.

source: Amabile (1982) Social psychology of creativity: a consensual assessment technique (as cited in Baer 2004 and LitBench)
finding: Founding paper of the CAT: experts judge creative products independently, using their own sense of creativity, with no definitions or rubric. Known only through citing papers I opened.
numbers: Baer 2004 states that CAT alphas typically exceed .70 and often reach the .90s.
limits: Original not opened.
agent_relevance: The CAT is the human gold standard: independent expert ratings, aggregated and checked by inter-rater reliability. Our validation sets should copy that.
